paragraphs: Compressing a language model can leave its overall benchmark accuracy almost unchanged while substantially changing which questions it answers correctly. This paper studies these changes, called flips. Correct answers can become incorrect while previously incorrect answers become correct, allowing the two effects to cancel in the aggregate score.

The authors examine this behavior across multiple compression techniques, models, and datasets. Their central concern is the difference between preserving a numerical score and preserving the behavior users encounter. They also evaluate free-form generation with MT-Bench, using both qualitative and quantitative assessments. In those evaluations, compressed models with many flips perform worse than their uncompressed counterparts.

The paper argues that accuracy and perplexity remain necessary but do not fully characterize compression quality. It proposes supplementing them with two measures of distance from the original model: flips and KL-divergence. The authors find these measures are well correlated. The practical implication is that evaluating compression should include how much behavior changes, alongside how well the compressed model scores overall.
neurips-2024-accuracy-is-not-all-you-nee.tldr: Compression can preserve overall accuracy while changing many answers, motivating evaluation with behavioral distance measures.

paragraphs: Reasoning examples in a prompt can contain irrelevant statements or incorrect steps. This paper asks how reliably language models reason when their examples contain that noise. The authors create NoRa, a dataset designed to evaluate this setting, and find widespread vulnerability among the models studied. Self-correction and self-consistency offer only limited protection.

Relative to clean reasoning examples, the reported accuracy drops range from 1.4% to 19.8% for irrelevant thoughts and from 2.2% to 40.4% for inaccurate thoughts. The proposed response, CD-CoT, uses external guidance in the form of one clean rationale. It contrasts that example with noisy rationales to help distinguish useful reasoning from contamination.

CD-CoT works on both the prompt and the resulting answers. It rephrases and selects rationales to clean up the input, then explores multiple reasoning paths and votes on their answers. Experiments report an average accuracy improvement of 17.8% over the base model and stronger denoising than the compared methods. These findings support combining a small amount of clean supervision with reasoning diversity.
neurips-2024-can-language-models-perform.tldr: CD-CoT uses one clean reasoning example to help language models handle noisy demonstrations and improve answer accuracy.

paragraphs: Text embeddings are useful for predicting how the brain responds to language, but their numerical features can be difficult to interpret. This paper introduces question-answering embeddings, or QA-Emb, in which every feature corresponds to an answer to a yes-or-no question posed to a language model. The questions give the representation an explicit, readable meaning.

Training this representation centers on choosing its questions rather than learning model weights. The authors use the resulting features to build models that predict fMRI voxel responses to language stimuli. This makes the choice of semantic properties part of the model design: researchers can examine the questions defining the feature space when interpreting its predictions.

QA-Emb significantly outperforms an established interpretable baseline while using very few questions. The authors also find that an efficient model can approximate these embeddings effectively, and they explore applications to simple language-processing tasks. The neuroscience result supports using question-defined features to formulate and evaluate ideas about semantic brain representations, with predictive performance and feature interpretability built into the same approach.
neurips-2024-crafting-interpretable-embe.tldr: QA-Emb turns answers to selected yes-or-no questions into interpretable text features for predicting brain responses to language.

paragraphs: Language-model alignment commonly begins by teaching a model to imitate human demonstrations, followed by preference learning with a reward model. This paper asks whether reward learning can also improve that first supervised fine-tuning stage. Its approach extracts a reward signal from demonstrations while simultaneously learning the model that produces responses.

The method uses inverse reinforcement learning to jointly construct a reward model and a policy model from the demonstration data. The resulting fine-tuning algorithms are described as efficient to implement and robust to low-quality supervised examples. The authors also establish a connection with Self-Play Fine-tune, linking their reward-learning formulation to an existing family of alignment methods.

The theoretical result establishes convergence to stationary solutions of the inverse reinforcement learning problem, rather than claiming globally optimal solutions. Experiments align models with 1 billion and 7 billion parameters and evaluate them using a reward benchmark model and the HuggingFace Open LLM Leaderboard. The reported improvements over existing supervised fine-tuning approaches support using demonstrations for reward learning as well as imitation.
neurips-2024-getting-more-juice-out-of-t.tldr: Learning rewards and response policies together from human demonstrations improves supervised fine-tuning in the reported alignment experiments.

paragraphs: Rendering a changing scene with Gaussian splatting requires predicting how its representation deforms over time. Popular approaches encode space and time using planes. This paper argues that their low-rank assumption and extensive decomposition create excessive overlap among features, limiting the quality of the resulting images.

Grid4D replaces that representation with a decomposition of four-dimensional space-time into one spatial and three temporal three-dimensional hash encodings. This avoids the low-rank assumption identified in the plane-based methods. A directional attention module then combines spatial and temporal features, using spatial information to help fit the different deformations occurring in distinct parts of a scene.

The model also includes a smoothness regularizer to stabilize deformation predictions, addressing a lack of smoothness in explicit representations. Together, the encoding, attention, and regularization target how motion is represented and coordinated across the scene. Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art models in both visual quality and rendering speed, supporting the proposed representation for the dynamic scenes evaluated.
neurips-2024-grid4d-4d-decomposed-hash-e.tldr: Grid4D combines decomposed hash encodings, directional attention, and smoothness regularization to improve dynamic Gaussian rendering.

paragraphs: Machine-learned interatomic potentials help make accurate atomistic simulations more affordable. A key design principle is equivariance: model representations should transform consistently when an atomic system is rotated or reflected. Many successful message-passing models implement this principle with spherical tensors, whose products involve complicated numerical coefficients and can be computationally demanding.

This paper develops an alternative using higher-rank irreducible Cartesian tensors. Existing Cartesian approaches offer promise but constrain how messages can be constructed, limiting architectural flexibility and expressive power. The authors integrate irreducible Cartesian tensor products into message-passing networks to address those restrictions and broaden the available mechanisms for representing atomic interactions.

The work combines formal and empirical evidence. It proves that the resulting layers preserve equivariance and the required traceless property. Across several benchmark datasets, the models consistently match or outperform state-of-the-art spherical and Cartesian models. These results support the proposed tensor construction as a flexible, competitive foundation for interatomic modeling, without establishing a universal advantage for every simulation setting.
neurips-2024-higher-rank-irreducible-car.tldr: Higher-rank Cartesian tensor products enable flexible equivariant message-passing layers that match or improve on leading atomistic models.

paragraphs: A priority queue maintains elements with assigned priorities and supports two central operations: inserting a new element and extracting the element with the highest priority. This paper studies how predictions can help perform those operations more efficiently. It places this familiar data structure within the learning-augmented framework, where predictive information may be useful even though it can be inaccurate.

The authors examine three prediction models covering different use cases. For each, the question is how the queue's algorithm can use the available predictions to improve operational performance. Treating predictions as potentially imperfect is part of the formulation, so the problem concerns algorithm design with uncertain guidance rather than assuming that future behavior is known exactly.

The paper shows how these prediction models can enhance priority-queue operations and establishes optimality of its solution within the studied framework. It also discusses possible applications. Its contribution is therefore both a set of methods for incorporating predictions into a fundamental data structure and a theoretical account of the performance those methods can achieve.
neurips-2024-learning-augmented-priority.tldr: The paper develops and analyzes priority queues that use potentially inaccurate predictions to improve operation performance.

paragraphs: Determining whether a language model trained on a particular text is difficult when apparent evidence of memorization can instead reflect differences between data distributions. This paper shows that membership inference can look successful when training examples are compared with nonmembers from a different distribution, such as more recent articles. Most tested methods fall to chance-level performance when that mismatch is removed.

The authors shift the question from individual passages to collections of documents. Their dataset inference method selects membership-inference techniques that provide useful signals for the distribution being examined, then aggregates those signals into a statistical test. This accommodates the finding that different techniques work on different kinds of text.

On different subsets of the Pile, the method distinguishes training and test sets with reported p-values below 0.1 and no false positives in those evaluations. The result supports assessing evidence across a dataset rather than relying on a single passage. It also highlights that distribution matching is essential to interpreting whether a detected signal actually concerns training membership.
neurips-2024-llm-dataset-inference-did-y.tldr: Dataset inference combines distribution-specific membership signals to test whether a collection of texts was used in language-model training.

paragraphs: Useful image features should recognize the same physical location across different camera views while distinguishing it from other locations. Doing this under large viewpoint changes requires more than recognizing object categories: the representation must also capture relationships in three dimensions. Existing approaches train this ability as patch retrieval, matching patches that originate from the same 3D location.

The obstacle addressed here is the cost of the training objective. Earlier formulations require substantial memory and computation, limiting large-scale training. LoCo reformulates and approximates the smooth average precision objective used for ranking retrieved patches. The resulting loss improves memory efficiency by three orders of magnitude and allows much larger models to be trained with the same computational resources.

The authors evaluate the learned features directly on consistency across multiple views and through scene-stable panoptic segmentation. They report significantly better results than the previous state of the art. The contribution links a more economical training objective to improved representations: reducing the memory bottleneck makes it possible to train stronger features for recognizing locations consistently.
neurips-2024-loco-learning-3d-location-c.tldr: LoCo greatly reduces ranking-loss memory use to train stronger image features that recognize the same 3D locations across views.

paragraphs: Evaluating a latent representation involves understanding how much diversity its points contain and how that diversity changes with the scale of observation. This paper uses metric-space magnitude, a mathematical quantity describing a space's effective size across scales. Magnitude also captures geometric properties associated with curvature, density, and entropy.

The authors develop a family of diversity measures based on this quantity. They also formalize a way to compare the magnitude functions of finite metric spaces, allowing different representations to be assessed through their multiscale structure. The measures are efficiently computable and provably stable under data perturbations, giving the comparison a mathematical foundation beyond a single diversity score.

The work evaluates these measures for automated diversity estimation, detection of mode collapse, and assessment of generative models producing text, images, and graphs. The authors report superior performance across the investigated domains and tasks. These results support magnitude as a practical tool for examining whether representations or generated outputs preserve varied structure, with comparisons that incorporate multiple scales of distance.
neurips-2024-metric-space-magnitude-for-.tldr: Magnitude-based measures provide stable, efficient comparisons of representation diversity across multiple scales.

paragraphs: Many vision models arrange their internal tokens on a grid tied to image coordinates. For video, this encourages a token to represent a particular position even as scene elements move through it. Moving Off-the-Grid, or MooG, explores representations whose organization can instead remain associated with moving scene structures.

The model combines cross-attention with positional embeddings to separate the arrangement of its internal representation from the arrangement of the image. It learns through next-frame prediction on video data. The authors find that this simple self-supervised objective produces latent tokens that attach to particular scene structures and track them as they move across the image.

To assess whether those representations are useful beyond prediction, the authors train readout models on top of them for several downstream tasks. Both qualitative observations and quantitative evaluations support their usefulness compared with grid-based baselines. The result suggests that loosening the connection between token identity and image position can provide a strong foundation for vision tasks involving persistent scene information.
neurips-2024-moving-off-the-grid-scene-g.tldr: MooG learns video tokens that follow scene structures over time instead of remaining tied to fixed image locations.

paragraphs: Learning among players with competing interests can keep changing indefinitely, even when each player uses a no-regret algorithm. This paper studies that behavior in generalized harmonic games, extending beyond the narrower setting of two-player zero-sum games. It focuses on follow-the-regularized-leader, or FTRL, a widely studied family of learning rules.

The authors show that continuous-time FTRL dynamics are recurrent: they return arbitrarily close to their starting point infinitely often and fail to converge. The ordinary discrete-time implementation can behave worse, potentially trapping players in an endless cycle of best responses. These results explain why a familiar learning rule need not settle strategic interaction in this class of games.

Adding a suitable extrapolation step changes the outcome. The analyzed family includes optimistic and mirror-prox variants of FTRL, and it converges to a Nash equilibrium from any initial condition while guaranteeing each player at most constant regret. Within the studied game class and update framework, the result connects a specific algorithmic modification to both stable long-run behavior and strong regret guarantees.
neurips-2024-no-regret-learning-in-harmo.tldr: Suitable extrapolation makes FTRL converge in generalized harmonic games, where its standard dynamics can recur or cycle.

paragraphs: Semi-implicit variational inference builds flexible probability approximations by combining a kernel with a mixing distribution. Existing approaches often represent the mixing distribution implicitly, making the resulting density intractable. That prevents direct optimization of the evidence lower bound, or ELBO, and motivates alternatives involving additional bounds, costly inner sampling loops, or minimax objectives.

Particle Variational Inference represents the mixing distribution with an empirical collection of particles. The target mixing distribution is characterized through minimization of a free-energy functional, and the particle method arises from a Euclidean–Wasserstein gradient flow. This construction directly optimizes the ELBO without assuming a parametric form for the mixing distribution.

Experiments show favorable performance against other semi-implicit variational inference methods across several tasks. The authors also analyze a related free-energy gradient flow, establishing existence and uniqueness of solutions and propagation-of-chaos results. The theoretical claims concern that related flow, while the empirical comparisons support the particle algorithm. Together, they offer a computational approach and mathematical grounding for flexible variational inference.
neurips-2024-particle-semi-implicit-vari.tldr: Particle Variational Inference uses particles to directly optimize the ELBO without a parametric assumption on the mixing distribution.

paragraphs: Iteratively reweighted least squares recovers a signal through a sequence of weighted fitting problems, updating the weights after each step. Related algorithms also appear in feature learning and linear neural networks. This paper develops a common asymptotic analysis for a family containing classical IRLS, lin-RFM, and alternating minimization for linear diagonal networks.

The analysis uses a batched setting with independent, identically distributed Gaussian covariates. Under this formulation, the authors show that a suitably chosen reweighting policy can produce favorable performance within only a handful of iterations. The result identifies weight selection as an important ingredient in the behavior shared by these otherwise differently motivated algorithms.

The authors also extend the analysis to group-sparse recovery, where useful signal structure involves groups of coordinates. Incorporating that grouping into the reweighting scheme provably improves test error relative to reweighting coordinates individually. Within the stated setting, this gives a precise reason to design the weight updates around known signal structure and connects that design choice to prediction quality.
neurips-2024-precise-asymptotics-of-rewe.tldr: A unified analysis shows how suitable reweighting can yield rapid progress and exploit group sparsity to improve test error.

paragraphs: Preference learning tries to infer the hidden utilities behind people's choices. That inference depends on how choices are modeled, but human decisions can change with the context in which options are compared. Cognitive models capture some of these effects, yet their computational difficulty has encouraged practical systems to use simpler Bradley-Terry variants.

This paper constructs a tractable surrogate for a state-of-the-art cognitive model. It introduces a procedure for fitting the surrogate to human observations and extends the model to handle data that the original cognitive account cannot explain. The aim is to retain richer descriptions of human choice while making them usable inside preference-learning systems.

On large-scale human data, the proposed model gives significantly better utility inferences than existing Bradley-Terry variants, both with fixed datasets and with actively elicited observations. Separately, simulations show significant utility improvements across a range of real-world task settings. The evidence links better modeling of contextual choice behavior to better inference, with downstream decision benefits demonstrated in simulation.
neurips-2024-preference-learning-of-late.tldr: A tractable surrogate for a richer cognitive choice model improves preference inference and simulated decision utility.

paragraphs: Image stitching commonly uses three successive stages: aligning images, fusing their content, and producing a rectangular result. When each stage has its own trained network, errors can propagate through the sequence, and the coupled components become difficult to tune. SRStitcher simplifies the latter two stages by expressing them as a single inpainting problem.

The authors reformulate fusion and rectangling so that a pretrained diffusion model can perform both together. Weighted masks guide the model's reverse generation process, directing how the integrated inpainting task is carried out. The method needs no additional model training or fine-tuning and completes the combined task in one inference.

This changes the organization of the stitching pipeline: two interacting processing stages become one coordinated operation, while registration remains a separate part of the setup. Extensive experiments support the unified model's interpretability and generalization, and report better performance and stability than state-of-the-art methods. The findings show that reusing a pretrained generative model can simplify this portion of stitching while improving the evaluated outputs.
neurips-2024-reconstructing-the-image-st.tldr: SRStitcher combines image fusion and rectangling into one guided diffusion-inpainting task without additional training.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must build a policy from an existing collection of behavior. When that collection comes from multiple experts, some demonstrations may be suboptimal. The paper focuses on the need to combine the strongest behaviors available in the dataset, rather than treating every demonstrated action as equally desirable.

The authors formulate this selection problem through optimal transport. Their algorithm seeks a policy that maps a state to a partial distribution of the best expert actions available for that state. Using a partial distribution makes selective use of the recorded behavior central to the formulation. The learning target is therefore shaped around the useful portions of the expert data.

The method is evaluated on continuous-control problems in the D4RL suite, where the authors report improvements over existing methods. These results support optimal transport as a way to organize the stitching of good behaviors in offline learning. The contribution joins a new formulation with an algorithm aimed at extracting an effective policy from demonstrations of mixed quality.
neurips-2024-rethinking-optimal-transpor.tldr: An optimal-transport formulation learns policies by selectively combining strong actions from mixed-quality offline demonstrations.

paragraphs: Strong branching is an effective but expensive heuristic for solving mixed-integer linear programs. Message-passing graph neural networks are often trained to approximate its scores cheaply. This paper asks whether those networks can represent the desired scores at all, showing that their capacity depends on the class of optimization problems they encounter.

The authors define an MP-tractable class and prove a universal approximation result within it. For any data distribution over that class, an appropriate message-passing network can approximate strong-branching scores to arbitrarily high accuracy and probability. Outside that class, a comparable general guarantee is impossible: some problem instances have different scores but cannot be distinguished by any such network, regardless of parameter count.

The paper then studies second-order folklore graph neural networks. With this architecture, the approximation theorem extends to the full space of mixed-integer linear programs. A small-scale numerical experiment directly supports the theoretical findings. The central implication concerns representation: changing the network structure can overcome a limitation that simply enlarging an ordinary message-passing network cannot remove.
neurips-2024-rethinking-the-capacity-of-.tldr: Standard message-passing networks cannot represent every strong-branching score, while a second-order architecture supports a broader approximation guarantee.

paragraphs: Inverse rendering aims to separate a scene's observed appearance into factors such as lighting and material properties. Strong illumination complicates that separation because shadows and reflections can be confused with properties of the object itself. RobIR addresses this problem with an implicit neural representation designed for brightly lit scenes.

The method combines ACES tone mapping with regularized visibility estimation to reconstruct the object's reflectance behavior. It jointly models indirect radiance, surface normals, visibility, and direct light. Accounting for these components together is intended to separate environmental illumination from the object's physically based materials without imposing strict scene constraints.

The authors report recovery of high-quality albedo and roughness even when the scene contains strong lighting, shadows, and specular reflections, with recovered materials free of shadow interference. RobIR also outperforms existing methods in quantitative and qualitative evaluations. The findings support joint treatment of illumination and visibility as a way to reduce lighting contamination in material estimates, addressing a central ambiguity in the evaluated inverse-rendering settings.
neurips-2024-robir-robust-inverse-render.tldr: RobIR jointly models lighting and visibility to recover material properties from strongly illuminated scenes with shadows and reflections.

paragraphs: Human preference labels can be inconsistent or incorrect because of bias, ambiguous context, or insufficient annotator training. These errors can distort reward learning in reinforcement learning from human feedback. R³M addresses the problem by treating potentially corrupted labels as sparse outliers within the preference data.

The method expresses robust reward estimation as maximum likelihood with an ℓ1 regularization term. An alternating optimization algorithm solves the resulting problem with negligible additional computational overhead relative to standard RLHF. The framework can also be extended to preference optimization methods such as direct preference optimization, broadening where the outlier model can be used.

The theoretical guarantee is conditional: under appropriate regularity conditions, R³M consistently learns the underlying reward and identifies outliers when the number of corrupted labels grows sublinearly with the sample size. Experiments in robotic control and language generation show improved reward robustness under several forms of preference-data perturbation. Together, the results support explicitly modeling sparse corruption while specifying the regime in which reliable recovery is guaranteed.
neurips-2024-robust-reinforcement-learni.tldr: R³M models corrupted preference labels as sparse outliers to improve reward robustness, with recovery guarantees under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Preference optimization trains a language model to favor responses judged better than alternatives. SimPO simplifies this process by using a sequence's average log probability as its implicit reward. The paper argues that this quantity better matches generation behavior and removes the need for a separate reference model, reducing computation and memory requirements.

The method also adds a target reward margin to the Bradley-Terry objective. This encourages a larger separation between preferred and rejected responses. The authors compare SimPO with DPO and related methods across base and instruction-tuned models, including Mistral, Llama 3, and Gemma 2, using several chat evaluation benchmarks.

The reported improvements occur without a substantial increase in response length. SimPO exceeds DPO by up to 6.4 points on AlpacaEval 2 and 7.5 points on Arena-Hard. Its strongest reported Gemma-2-9B-it model achieves a 72.4% length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2 and 59.1% on Arena-Hard. These results support combining a reference-free reward with an explicit preference margin in the evaluated training setups.
neurips-2024-simpo-simple-preference-opt.tldr: SimPO uses average sequence log probability and a target reward margin to improve preference optimization without a reference model.

paragraphs: Extragradient methods are useful for minimax optimization, where one side minimizes an objective while another maximizes it. Their stochastic versions have been less successful in convex-concave problems, particularly without constraints. This paper investigates whether changing the order in which finite-sum components are processed can produce a convergent stochastic method.

The analysis finds that two ordering approaches, random reshuffling and flip-flop shuffling, can still diverge in unconstrained convex-concave problems. Shuffling alone therefore does not resolve the difficulty in the studied setting. The authors add an anchoring mechanism to flip-flop shuffling, yielding a method called SEG-FFA, and establish its convergence for convex-concave problems.

For the more restrictive strongly-convex-strongly-concave setting, the paper provides upper and lower bounds that demonstrate a faster convergence rate for SEG-FFA than other shuffling-based methods. The contribution distinguishes an unsuccessful ingredient on its own from a combination with provable benefits. It explains how anchoring can make a particular stochastic extragradient design converge and improve its rate under stronger curvature assumptions.
neurips-2024-stochastic-extragradient-wi.tldr: Combining flip-flop shuffling with anchoring yields a convergent stochastic extragradient method with provable rate improvements.

paragraphs: Generating a particular subject from reference images requires preserving its identity while responding to new text prompts. Methods focused heavily on reference similarity can involve costly training and risk overfitting. This paper introduces the λ-Harmonic reward to guide subject-driven generation, support model selection, and identify when to stop fine-tuning.

Combined with a Bradley-Terry preference model, the reward supplies preference labels for a method called Reward Preference Optimization. RPO uses only 3% of the negative samples used by DreamBooth and requires fewer gradient steps. It fine-tunes only the U-Net, achieving text-image alignment without training the text encoder or optimizing text embeddings.

Early stopping based on the reward is intended to speed training and regularize adaptation to the references. The authors find the reward reliable for model selection and report a state-of-the-art CLIP-I score of 0.833 alongside a CLIP-T score of 0.314 on DreamBench. The findings support using the same reward framework for preference supervision and training control in the evaluated subject-generation task.
neurips-2024-subject-driven-text-to-imag.tldr: RPO uses a reward-derived preference signal and early stopping to efficiently fine-tune subject-specific image generation.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines updates from participating devices through a server. This paper studies server-side extrapolation as a way to improve the convergence of FedProx. Although extrapolation has been useful in practice, the authors identify a gap in theoretical explanations and develop an optimizer called Extrapolated FedProx, or FedExProx.

The analysis covers three strategies for choosing extrapolation. One uses a constant choice determined by smoothness parameters and the number of participating devices. Two adapt to smoothness: FedExProx-GraDS uses gradient diversity, while FedExProx-StoPS uses a stochastic Polyak stepsize. These alternatives provide different ways to control how the server extends the update.

The theoretical setting is restricted to smooth convex or strongly convex problems in the interpolation regime. Within that setting, the paper studies improvements in convergence and supports its theory with carefully constructed numerical experiments. The contribution gives server extrapolation a more explicit mathematical foundation and relates its behavior to concrete strategy choices, with empirical corroboration tailored to the assumptions of the analysis.
neurips-2024-the-power-of-extrapolation-.tldr: FedExProx studies three server-extrapolation strategies with convergence analysis for smooth convex problems in the interpolation regime.

paragraphs: Adapting to a new distribution becomes especially difficult when only a few target examples are available and they fall outside the training data's support. This paper develops a theoretical account of when extrapolation is possible in that setting, without requiring an entire target distribution contained within the training distribution.

The authors use a latent-variable model built around minimal changes in causal mechanisms. This turns extrapolation into a question of identifying hidden variables. They establish conditions on the distribution shift and estimation objectives that permit identification even with a single target sample outside the training support. The result is conditional on those properties, rather than a general guarantee from one observation.

The theory also reveals how the smoothness of the underlying manifold interacts with the nature of the shift. These relationships inform the design of practical adaptation algorithms. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the theoretical findings and their practical implications, connecting a causal account of limited change to methods for adapting beyond previously observed data.
neurips-2024-towards-understanding-extra.tldr: A causal latent-variable framework identifies conditions that make extrapolation possible even from one off-support target sample.
